ask.q.display: RMT v3 vs MemGPT — what's the core difference, and why should I care?
ask.h1: RMT v3 vs MemGPT — what's the core difference, and why should I care?
ask.h2: Diagram the long-context route contest as a comparison table

ask.h7: How do GraphRAG and LightRAG differ on episodic memory?
ask.answer.lede.html: Your two saves (RMT v3, MemGPT) represent two fundamentally different paradigms for handling «context that exceeds training length» — a distinction that produces order-of-magnitude cost differences in production. Worth your attention.
ask.answer.p1.html: RMT v3 uses recurrent compression to stuff entire context into a fixed-length hidden state, holding O(n) at 2M tokens1; MemGPT treats the model itself as an «operating system», using explicit memory scheduling (main context ↔ recall storage) to swap in information as needed2. The former is «implicit compression baked into weights»; the latter is «explicit run-time paging».
ask.answer.h2: Three practical differences worth your attention
ask.answer.li1.html: Training vs inference-time opportunity cost: RMT v3 requires retraining or continued training of the base model1; MemGPT runs on frozen weights, in the same camp as the LongMem paper you saved on Apr 173.
ask.answer.li2.html: VRAM footprint: RMT v3's hidden-state memory is constant; MemGPT's main context is still bounded by standard KV cache — at 200K, KV cache reaches ~125 GB on a 70B model (your note #2204 from Apr 22 has the math).
ask.answer.li3.html: Failure modes: RMT v3 keeps compression loss ≤ 2.3% on narrative text, but Anthropic measured 14.7% on code and tabular tasks1; MemGPT's failure mode is «paging thrash» under bad scheduling — it needs engineering tuning.
ask.answer.p2.html: Worth noting: on May 3, Lilian Weng argued on her blog that even when the context fits, attention dilution still erodes multi-hop accuracy — hence «the promise of long windows is overstated in production»4. This indirectly supports MemGPT's engineering case.
ask.answer.curator.html: If you're building a conversational agent (multi-turn, long horizon), MemGPT gives you more control; if you're doing batch document analysis (one-shot long inputs), RMT v3's cost curve wins. Both will likely be unified under some two-tier hybrid architecture by 2026 H2.

brief.s1.label: 30s summary
brief.s1.body.html: Two heavy works landed in long-context this week: DeepMind's RMT v3 holds linear complexity at 2M tokens1; Anthropic reports Claude 3.5 at 99.4% accuracy on 200K needle tasks2. On the surface, technical breakthroughs; in practice, two conflicting routes — and evidence in your library already points to a third possibility (a two-tier hybrid).
brief.s2.h1.t: DeepMind releases Recurrent Memory Transformer v3
brief.s2.h1.d: Recurrent compression holds linear complexity at 2,097,152 tokens; outscores GPT-4-128K on LongBench-v2 by 11.2 pts.
brief.s2.h2.t: Claude 3.5 hits 99.4% on the 200K needle test
brief.s2.h2.d: Passes all 12 needle configurations; multi-hop subset at 73.1%.
brief.s2.h3.t: GraphRAG v0.4: 8K window + external memory wins 11 of 17
brief.s2.h3.d: Microsoft empirical: on long QA, «small window + strong retrieval» matches pure 200K.
brief.s3.p1.html: In the past 30 days, 412 pieces of literature evidence on long context entered your library. Most impactful: DeepMind's RMT v3 on May 71 and Anthropic's Claude 3.5 long-context report from the same week2. Both attack the same problem but along opposite paths — one uses compression to dodge the long-sequence cost, the other uses scaling to absorb it head-on.
brief.s3.p2.html: Your LongMem save from Apr 173 implies a third path: frozen base + external memory module. Microsoft's GraphRAG empirical study4 goes further: on 17 long-QA metrics, «small window + strong retrieval» matches pure 200K on 11. The real argument isn't «long vs short» — it's «where the information entropy is paid».
brief.s3.fig: Fig. 1 · The three routes on the «entropy–cost» plane · auto-generated by Curator.
brief.s4.kicker: § IV · DIALOGUE WITH YOUR EARLIER WORK
brief.s4.p.html: Your note #2204 «The real cost of long windows» from Apr 22 already pointed out: 200K KV cache memory is 25× that of 8K. This week, Lilian Weng's blog4 reaches the same verdict: «the promise of long windows is overstated in production». Your call from 22 days ago is now independently confirmed.
brief.s4.callout.body: «200K KV cache is 25× that of 8K» · Apr 22 · note #2204 — independently supported by Lilian Weng on May 3.
brief.s5.p1.html: Anthropic's rebuttal memo on May 85 argues that RMT v3's «≤ 2.3% compression loss» figure was measured on a narrative-text-biased set. On 1,200 code-completion tasks, the same compressor lost 14.7% in syntactically dense regions. This is the most worth-doubting detail in this week's headline work.
brief.s5.p2.html: The HELM v3 team6 simultaneously argues that needle-in-haystack as an evaluation has become too simple — multi-needle plus counterfactual needles should replace it. So Anthropic's 99.4% figure may itself be re-examined under new evaluation methodology.

topic.ov.h1: The long-context contest: explicit memory compression vs end-to-end attention scaling, divergence intensifies.
topic.ov.brief.label: EDITOR’S BRIEF · 30s summary
topic.ov.brief.body.html: Over the past 30 days this topic gathered 38 key claims and 412 pieces of evidence. Two main routes are diverging — Route A (DeepMind/Anthropic camp) argues for end-to-end attention window scaling; Route B (Microsoft Research/MemGPT camp) argues for external episodic memory in place of long windows. Curator's view: they are not mutually exclusive — H2 2026 will most likely converge on a «two-tier hybrid» architecture.
topic.ov.p1.html: Over the past 30 days, 412 pieces of literature evidence entered your library on long context. The most impactful: on May 7, DeepMind released Recurrent Memory Transformer v3, holding linear complexity at 2,097,152 tokens via recurrent compression1. The same week, Anthropic released Claude 3.5's needle-in-haystack at 200K — passing all 12 configurations at 99.4%2.
topic.ov.p2.html: Yet the alternative road implied by your LongMem save from Apr 173 — using an external memory module to «fake» long context — hasn't died. Microsoft Research's GraphRAG v0.4 experiment from May 34 shows that on 1M-token document QA, external memory + 8K window beat pure 200K on 11 of 17 metrics. The two routes win different task structures.
topic.ov.h3: Three disagreements you should know about
topic.ov.li1.html: Compression-loss debate —— the RMT v3 paper claims ≤ 2.3% compression loss, but the Anthropic team points out the test set is biased toward narrative text, understating losses for code and tabular long-context5.
topic.ov.li2.html: Retrieval-eval debate —— is needle-in-haystack still valid? The HELM v3 team argues single-needle is too easy now — replace it with multi-needle + counterfactual needles6.
topic.ov.li3.html: Inference-cost debate —— your note from Apr 22 «The real cost of long windows» already pointed out: in production, 200K-context KV cache memory is 25× that of 8K — and no headline work has confronted this yet.
